passages.title: A spreading vine
passages.text: Once found only in a few gardens, the vine has become ______ in the region: it now grows along nearly every roadside, fence line and riverbank.

passages.title: A plan with room to grow
passages.text: The architects' plan for the new campus was deliberately ______: by leaving large parts of the site unbuilt and designing roads that could be extended, it allowed the city to add buildings as future needs became clear.

passages.title: Grains from a geyser
passages.text: Plumes of water vapor erupting from Saturn's moon Enceladus contain salt and tiny grains of silica. On Earth, silica grains of that size typically form when water that is hot enough to dissolve rock cools rapidly. Researchers studying the plumes therefore concluded that ______

passages.title: A snail that stops flinching
passages.text: When a garden snail is tapped lightly on its shell, it pulls back into the shell. After many harmless taps in a row, however, it stops withdrawing. A biologist hypothesizes that the snail has learned that the taps are harmless, rather than simply becoming too tired to withdraw.

passages.title: Lamps and insects
passages.text:
Researchers placed insect traps beneath three kinds of outdoor lighting for one summer and counted the insects caught per trap each night.
Lighting | Average insects per trap per night
White LED lamp | 120
Amber LED lamp | 45
No lamp | 10
The researchers concluded that switching from white to amber lamps would greatly reduce, but not eliminate, the extra insects that outdoor lighting attracts.

passages.title: The end of Norse Greenland (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Norse settlers lived in Greenland for nearly five hundred years before their settlements were abandoned in the 1400s. Many historians have attributed the abandonment mainly to a cooling climate, which shortened growing seasons and made it harder to keep livestock.
Text 2
Other historians point out that the settlements depended heavily on exporting walrus ivory to Europe. As European demand for walrus ivory fell in the 1300s and 1400s, they argue, the settlements lost the trade that had paid for imported goods, leaving them less able to withstand hard years.

passages.title: A blast over Siberia
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• On June 30, 1908, a huge explosion occurred over a remote forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia.
• It flattened an estimated 80 million trees over more than 2,000 square kilometers.
• Scientists reached the area for the first time in 1927.
• They expected to find a crater made by a meteorite but found none.
• Most scientists now think a space rock exploded in the air above the forest before it could reach the ground.

passages.title: A library built for efficiency
passages.text: The new public library was designed to use far less energy than the building it replaced. ______ its roof is covered with solar panels, and its windows are angled to let in low winter sunlight while blocking the higher summer sun.

passages.title: A fish from the deep past
passages.text: The ______ a fish once thought to have died out with the dinosaurs—was found alive off the coast of South Africa in 1938.

passages.title: A council's decision
passages.text: The city council approved the new budget last week, but ______ decision to reduce library hours drew protests from parents and teachers.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it now grows along nearly every roadside, fence line and riverbank
candidates.explanation: Growing along 'nearly every' roadside and riverbank means the vine is found almost everywhere: "ubiquitous."

A.rationale: A plant growing almost everywhere is the opposite of endangered.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the vine has stopped growing.

C.rationale: The vine began in gardens, but the colon describes how widespread it has become, not its use.

hints: How widespread is the vine now?
candidates.remember: The explanation after a colon usually defines the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: allowed the city to add buildings as future needs became clear
candidates.explanation: A plan that leaves room for unplanned additions is not fixed in advance: it is "open-ended."

B.rationale: Leaving land unbuilt is restraint, not lavish spending.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the plan follows a standard pattern.

D.rationale: A plan built to be extended later is not finished.

hints: Was the plan meant to be complete or to change?
candidates.remember: Use the purpose clause to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the silica grains were probably carried to Enceladus by meteorites.
choices.B: water beneath the moon's surface is likely heated in contact with rock.
choices.C: the plumes are made mostly of silica rather than of water vapor.
choices.D: the surface of Enceladus is warmer than the surface of Earth.

candidates.evidence: water that is hot enough to dissolve rock cools rapidly
candidates.explanation: On Earth, such grains come from hot water that dissolved rock and then cooled. Finding them in the plumes suggests the moon's water was heated in contact with rock, probably on the floor of its ocean.

A.rationale: The text links the grains to hot water on the moon, not to outside sources.

C.rationale: The text says the plumes are water vapor that contains grains, not mostly silica.

D.rationale: The reasoning concerns hot water below, not the surface temperature.

hints: How do grains like these form on Earth?

strategy.explanation: Apply the Earth explanation to Enceladus.

candidates.remember: When a text gives a known cause on Earth, apply it to the new setting.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (supporting a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the biologist's hypothesis?

choices.A: Snails stopped withdrawing more quickly when the taps came closer together.
choices.B: Snails that were tapped many times moved more slowly for an hour afterward.
choices.C: Snails that ignored taps still withdrew at once from a new kind of touch.
choices.D: Snails withdrew into their shells when they were first tapped on the shell.

candidates.evidence: rather than simply becoming too tired to withdraw
candidates.explanation: A tired snail would not withdraw from anything. If snails that ignore taps still withdraw quickly from a new touch, they can still withdraw, so the lack of response to taps must reflect learning that taps are harmless.

A.rationale: Faster stopping with closer taps fits tiredness just as well as learning.

B.rationale: Slower movement suggests tiredness, which is the alternative the hypothesis rejects.

D.rationale: This describes the starting behavior and does not distinguish learning from tiredness.

hints: What would a tired snail fail to do?

strategy.explanation: Ask which finding rules out tiredness.

candidates.remember: To support one explanation, find evidence the rival explanation cannot account for.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Amber lamps drew 35 more insects than no lamp, compared with 110 more for white lamps.
choices.B: White LED lamps caught more insects per trap than either amber lamps or no lamp.
choices.C: Traps with no lamp caught an average of only 10 insects per night.
choices.D: Amber LED lamps caught 45 insects per trap per night on average.

candidates.evidence: greatly reduce, but not eliminate, the extra insects
candidates.explanation: The 'extra' insects are those beyond the no-lamp baseline: 120 - 10 = 110 for white and 45 - 10 = 35 for amber. Amber cuts the extra from 110 to 35 (a large reduction) but not to zero.

B.rationale: This shows white lamps attract the most but does not show how much amber reduces the extra insects or that some remain.

C.rationale: A single value does not compare the two kinds of lamps.

D.rationale: This value alone does not show the reduction or what remains compared with no lamp.

hints: What is the baseline for 'extra' insects?

strategy.explanation: Subtract the no-lamp count from each lamp count.

candidates.remember: An 'extra' amount is measured against a baseline.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the historians in Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation described in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that Greenland's climate may not have grown colder during that period
choices.B: By suggesting that the settlers may have left because they could no longer hunt walruses
choices.C: By agreeing that climate alone explains why the settlements were abandoned
choices.D: By arguing that a loss of trade may have mattered alongside the colder climate

candidates.evidence: leaving them less able to withstand hard years
candidates.explanation: Text 2 adds the collapse of the ivory trade, which left the settlements 'less able to withstand hard years' such as cold ones. So it would treat economic loss as a cause alongside climate, not instead of it.

A.rationale: Text 2 does not dispute the cooling; it adds another cause.

B.rationale: Text 2 is about falling European demand for ivory, not about hunting.

C.rationale: Text 2 adds an economic cause, so it does not agree that climate alone explains it.

hints: Does Text 2 deny the cooling or add to it?

strategy.explanation: Note whether each text excludes the other's cause.

candidates.remember: Adding a cause is different from rejecting another one.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why scientists think the object exploded in the air. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: An explosion near the Tunguska River in 1908 flattened an estimated 80 million trees in a remote forest.
choices.B: Because there was wide damage but no crater, most scientists now think a space rock burst in the air.
choices.C: Scientists reached the Tunguska area for the first time in 1927, almost twenty years later.
choices.D: Most scientists now think that a space rock exploded above the forest near the Tunguska River.

candidates.evidence: They expected to find a crater made by a meteorite but found none.
candidates.explanation: Explaining why requires the evidence (widespread damage but no crater) and the conclusion (an explosion in the air). Only B gives both.

A.rationale: This describes the damage but does not explain why scientists think it was an airburst.

C.rationale: This gives a date but no reasoning about the explosion.

D.rationale: This states the conclusion without the evidence that explains it.

hints: Which choice includes both the evidence and the conclusion?

strategy.explanation: Check that the choice explains, not just states.

candidates.remember: To explain a conclusion, include the evidence that leads to it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: its roof is covered with solar panels
candidates.explanation: The second sentence gives particular features that show how the library saves energy, so "Specifically" fits.

A.rationale: The second sentence supports the first rather than contrasting with it.

B.rationale: The features are not a replacement for the design goal; they carry it out.

D.rationale: The features belong to the new library, not to an earlier time.

hints: Does the second sentence give details of the first?
candidates.remember: Use "specifically" when the next sentence gives the details of a general claim.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: was found alive off the coast of South Africa in 1938
candidates.explanation: The phrase "a fish once thought to have died out with the dinosaurs" interrupts the sentence and closes with a dash, so it must open with a matching dash.

A.rationale: The phrase that follows closes with a dash, so it must open with a dash, not a comma.

B.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate a subject from the phrase describing it.

C.rationale: Without an opening dash, the closing dash has nothing to pair with.

hints: How does the interrupting phrase end?
candidates.remember: Paired punctuation must match: dash with dash.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The city council approved the new budget last week
candidates.explanation: The pronoun refers to "the city council," a single body, so the singular possessive "its" is correct.

B.rationale: "Council" is a single body, so it takes the singular "its."

hints: What does the pronoun refer to?

strategy.explanation: Find the antecedent and match its number.

candidates.remember: A collective noun acting as one body takes "its."
